description: I'm Dawit, an Ethiopian full-stack dev (Next.js, offline apps, Amharic UI). We're doing Field Shift: an app using NASA rainfall data to show Ethiopian farmers how their rains changed and suggest crop rotations (teff, chickpea, faba bean) that fit. Amharic, offline, map + AI. Research done, ready to build. Looking for: Python/NASA data or GIS, agronomy/soil knowledge, UI design + video, Amharic writing. Any level welcome if you can commit the weekend! 🇪🇹
summary:
Zer · ዘር ("seed" in Amharic) is a web app that tells a farmer what their field should grow next. It turns 25 years of NASA Earth observations into one clear decision.

Pick any field on Earth on a live NASA satellite map: Blue Marble, plus Landsat/Sentinel-2 photos back to 2013. Zer reads NASA POWER weather and soil moisture, GPM IMERG rainfall, SRTM terrain and MODIS crop greenness. It then finds when the growing season really starts, replays 19 crops through every real season since 2001, and compares the farmer's current crop rotation with the two best alternatives. Each option shows what you gain, what it costs, how risky it is, and how sure we are.

A machine-learning model trained on 8,314 seasons from 327 places worldwide estimates the risk of a poor season, and its accuracy was tested honestly on regions it never saw.

This addresses Field Shift directly. Climate change has moved the farming calendar, and farmers who plant by habit now lose whole seasons. Zer works in English and Amharic, runs offline on a phone, and gives smallholders and extension officers NASA's knowledge in plain language.
details:
What it does and how it works

Zer · ዘር ("seed" in Amharic) helps a farmer decide what their field should grow next. It does this by turning 25 years of NASA Earth observations into a plain-language comparison.

  1. Choose a field. A live satellite map shows NASA Blue Marble when zoomed out and the farmer's real fields when zoomed in. "On a date" shows the NASA HLS Landsat/Sentinel-2 photo (30 m) for any month since 2013, and Zer picks the clearest, cloud-free pass. Users can choose one of 11 showcase farms (5 in Ethiopia, 6 on other continents), tap any point on land, or use their location.
  2. Describe the farm: soil, slope, rain-fed or irrigated, the current rotation, and the farmer's priorities.
  3. Climate engine. It finds when the growing season really starts each year (rain onset, or the frost-free window) and runs a daily soil-water balance (FAO-56 / FEWS NET WRSI). It also shows trends honestly, including "no clear trend" when there is none.
  4. Crop engine. Each of 19 crops is planted at its best date in every real year since 2001 and marked good, weak or failed, with the reason.
  5. Rotation engine. It searches every suitable 3-year rotation, applies agronomy rules (legumes, avoiding repeated cereals, cover crops), and compares the current rotation with the two best alternatives. Every score has an uncertainty range and a confidence label.
  6. Season Replay plays each option through all 25 real seasons with the same weather, so the only difference is the choice of crops.
  7. SI model. Gradient-boosted trees were trained on 8,314 growing seasons from 327 cropland places in 14 world regions. They predict the risk of a poor season from 19 NASA weather features and give the reasons for each prediction. We scored the model only on regions, places and years it never saw. It beats simpler models on unseen regions (AUC 0.61) and unseen places (0.63), but not on future years, and we report that openly. Its probabilities are well calibrated.
  8. Ask Zer, an AI assistant, explains the results in English or Amharic using only the numbers Zer computed.

Benefits

  • Works for any field on Earth, and covers Ethiopia in depth.
  • Shows trade-offs (food, income, soil, water, fertilizer, risk) instead of a single "best" answer.
  • Honest about uncertainty: ranges, confidence reasons, and stated model limits.
  • Bilingual (English and Amharic, with the Ethiopian calendar in Amharic), works on a phone, and works offline once a farm has been visited.
  • Free to use, with no NASA login needed.

Intended impact

Climate change is moving planting calendars. Smallholders who plant by habit lose whole seasons to late rains, frost or erosion. Zer brings NASA's 25-year record to farmers and to the extension officers (Development Agents in Ethiopia) who advise them. The goal is fewer failed seasons, healthier soil through legume rotations, and better use of scarce water and fertilizer.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: TypeScript, Python, JavaScript (Node.js).
  • App: Next.js 16, React 19 and Tailwind CSS 4, built as a progressive web app. Charts and the satellite map are hand-made, with no map or chart libraries.
  • Machine learning: Python with scikit-learn. The trained trees are exported to JSON and run in the browser, so they also work offline.
  • AI chat: an LLM accessed through OpenRouter.
  • NASA data:
    • POWER (weather, root-zone soil moisture)
    • GPM IMERG v07 (rain)
    • SRTM GL3 (terrain)
    • MODIS MOD13Q1 / MOD13A3 NDVI (greenness)
    • GIBS imagery (Blue Marble, MODIS, HLS Landsat/Sentinel-2, land cover)
  • Other data: Esri World Imagery, geoBoundaries.
  • Workflow: GitLab, Playwright for automated screenshots and checks.
  • Hardware: none; only a laptop and a phone.

Creativity

  • "Season Replay" makes 25 years of satellite data easy to grasp: each square is one real season, played through each choice of crops.
  • Automatic clearest-pass search finds a cloud-free Landsat/Sentinel-2 photo of the farmer's own field.
  • A machine-learning model that explains itself runs entirely in the browser.
  • The AI only explains Zer's own numbers, so it cannot invent data.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty: we report weak results and limits in plain words instead of overselling.
  • Language and literacy: short sentences in English and Amharic.
  • Accessibility: colour is always paired with a symbol (✓ ~ ×), and light and dark modes are both supported.
  • Unreliable internet and low-cost phones.
  • Respect for local knowledge: Zer supports the farmer and their extension officer, and never replaces their judgment.
